newsitem.title: CHINA: China cotton output may fall, state price unchanged.
newsitem.headline: China cotton output may fall, state price unchanged.

text.p: China's cotton output is expected to fall to about 4.0 million tonnes in 1997 and the government has decided not to adjust the state purchase price this year, officials said on Friday.
"Cotton output could reach about 4.0 million tonnes this year," said an official of the All-China Association of Supply and Marketing Cooperatives, which oversees state cotton purchases.
China produced 4.2 million tonnes of cotton in 1996, down by 11.7 percent from the previous year, official figures showed.
Official media have estimated 1997 acreage under cotton at 4.56 million hectares -- the lowest level in 10 years -- down by 4.2 percent from last year.
Chinese officials have said that expanding areas under grain, a key factor in bumper grain harvests in recent years, had led to falling acreage under cotton.
The government has decided not to raise the state cotton purchase price in 1997, the association official said. "The state purchase price will not be changed.
"Cotton supply has already exceeded demand," the official said by telephone. "Shortfalls are unlikely to occur in the near future."
China raised the state purchase price for standard ginned cotton to 700 yuan per 50 kg from 544 yuan per 50 kg in September 1995 to lure more farmers from higher-earning cash crops.
"Current state cotton purchase prices are too high," an official of the Ministry of Agriculture said. "Textiles firms will be unable to endure if prices to rise further."
But China's ailing textile industry, hit by a slump in exports in recent years, were buying cotton from state cotton firms at prices much lower than the government-set prices.
The government charged about 19,800 yuan per tonne for high-grade cotton, she said.
"We don't buy cotton at state allocated prices," an official of a Beijing-based state textile firm said. "We buy cotton at negotiated prices.
"Cotton firms are forced to sell their stockpiles," she said, indicating a discount of 2,000 yuan per tonne were likely.
"But imported cotton is even cheaper," she said, but declined to give further details.
